analysis.one_liner: Fines insurers that deny 25% or more of claims and refunds the penalties to enrollees.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with one cosponsor in April 2026, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, and has received no further action, hearing, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the Secretary of Health and Human Services fine any health insurance issuer whose plan year shows claims denials of 25% or more of claims (excluding denials the Secretary finds were correctly made for fraud or lack of medical necessity). The fine starts at $10 million and grows by $2 million for each percentage point above 25%, and the money collected would be split among the people enrolled in the penalized plans. Insurers would also have to tell people, in plain terms, why a claim was denied as not medically necessary and report their denial rates to HHS each year [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in fully insured group or individual health plans, especially those whose claims get denied: they would receive a share of penalty money collected from high-denial insurers, and they would get a written explanation of the insurer's medical-necessity standards and why their care failed to meet them [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Penalties are distributed pro rata to individuals who were enrolled in the penalized plan during that year, so denial fines flow back to policyholders rather than to the Treasury [S2].

An insurer denying a claim for lack of medical necessity must give the patient the insurer's medical-necessity standards for the item or service and an explanation of why the care failed to meet them, information patients currently must demand themselves [S2].
Every insurer must report its annual claims-denial percentage to HHS, creating a public baseline for how often each plan says no [S2].
The penalty scales with how far an insurer's denial rate exceeds 25%, up to $10 million plus $2 million per percentage point, so the worst deniers face the largest fines [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance issuers offering fully insured group or individual coverage bear the fines and the new notice-and-reporting paperwork. Because insurers price to expected costs, some of the penalty expense would likely show up in premiums, and the refunds are limited to enrollees of plans actually penalized [S2].

drawbacks.text: The penalties are modest next to insurer finances: the base fine is $10 million with $2 million per percentage point over 25%, an amount small compared with the revenue of large national insurers, and the Secretary 'may' rather than 'must' impose it, leaving enforcement to the discretion of whoever runs HHS [S2].
Audits are only as extensive as the Secretary 'determines appropriate', so a reluctant administration could find few denial problems without violating the statute [S2].

A flat 25% denial-rate trigger does not distinguish between plans that attract unusually complex claims and plans that deny routinely, and other non-fraud denial grounds such as coding errors still count toward the trigger [S2].

Insurers would face higher expected costs, and because premiums are set to cover expected claims and regulatory exposure, part of the cost of the policy would likely be passed back to the people it is meant to help (general policy mechanism; the bill text sets the penalty and reporting requirements [S2]).

The measure reaches only health insurance issuers offering fully insured group or individual coverage, so denials in self-insured employer plans, which cover a large share of workers, fall outside it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is popular and straightforward: make insurers with very high denial rates pay their own enrollees, and force them to explain denials in writing. Its design limits the payoff. Fines are capped at amounts that are small for national carriers, enforcement is discretionary and audit-dependent, the trigger is a blunt denial-rate threshold, and self-insured employer plans are untouched. An honest supporter would call this a floor-raiser, not a fix for wrongful denials; an honest critic would note the penalty costs can cycle back into premiums. The bigger obstacle so far is political: two House Democrats introduced it, and the committee has not moved it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 22, 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Angie Craig (D-MN) introduced H.R. 8442 with one Democratic cosponsor on April 22, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and the action history shows no hearings, markups, or floor action since [S4].
With a two-member Democratic sponsorship in a House controlled by Republicans, the bill faces the common path of dying in committee without a vote [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, health insurers: no penalty, no transparency requirement, and no refund obligation has advanced, and the bill's only activity is a committee referral [S4].

for.name: Rep. Angie Craig
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create civil penalties for insurers with high claims-denial rates and refund the money to enrollees.

for.name: Rep. Ryan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only other member to sign on.

against.name: Rep. Brett Guthrie
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill; the committee's only action is the referral itself [S4].

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor are Democrats, and in a House with 223 Republicans the bill has drawn no Republican support and no committee action.

industries.note: Plans with denial rates of 25% or more face fines up to $10 million plus $2 million per percentage point above that, refunded to enrollees, plus written-denial and annual-reporting duties [S2]. Because insurers profit when claims are denied and costs are avoided, the bill's financial interest runs against the patients it would compensate; part of the fine cost would likely be priced back into premiums.

industries.industry: Physicians, hospitals, and other care providers
industries.note: Providers bear the burden of fighting and appealing denials today; public denial-rate reporting and penalty pressure on high-denial insurers would push more claims toward payment, aligning provider finances with patient access [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor and no committee action since April 2026, the bill will almost certainly expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a hearing or vote, the fate of most bills referred to committee without leadership backing.
